definition: Based on guesses or theories rather than on solid facts or evidence.
example: Without the original letters, any account of the poet's childhood remains speculative.
nuance: Speculative stresses a lack of supporting evidence, while hypothetical describes a case imagined for the sake of argument.
prompt: Scientists discuss a newly found fossil that consists of just one tooth.
options: With only a single tooth, any claim about the animal's diet is speculative.
The speculative findings had been confirmed by dozens of careful measurements.
The museum labeled the tooth speculative because it was so beautifully polished.
The team took a speculative look at the tooth through a magnifying glass.
reasons: One tooth gives too little evidence, so conclusions about diet must rest on guesswork.
Results backed by many measurements are well supported, the reverse of guesswork.
This confuses the word with spectacular; shine has nothing to do with uncertain reasoning.
The word describes ideas lacking proof, not the act of looking closely at something.

practice.prompt: A local reporter hears rumors that a neighborhood bakery will close.
options: Until the owner comments, talk of the bakery closing is purely speculative.
The owner's signed announcement made the exact closing date speculative.
The reporter was so speculative that she refused to guess about anything at all.
The bakery's speculative rye bread sold out early because it smelled so fresh.
reasons: Without confirmation from the owner, the rumor rests on guesses rather than facts.
An official signed statement is firm evidence, which removes the need to guess.
Refusing to guess is the opposite of reasoning from conjecture.
Bread's smell or freshness can't be based on theory; the word describes claims and ideas.
